genZNote: The mold that quietly changed the 20th century — an industrially improved relative of the strain Fleming stumbled onto is still used to manufacture penicillin at scale.

morphology.arrangement: Branching septate hyphae bearing brush-shaped conidiophores

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, decaying organic matter, and spoiled food
habitat.hostAssociation: Free-living environmental mold; extremely rare cause of human infection except in severely immunocompromised hosts
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Common indoor and outdoor mold, notorious for growing on spoiled bread, fruit, and cheese
habitat.reservoir: Soil, decaying plant material, indoor environments

microscopy.appearance: Septate hyphae with characteristic brush-shaped (penicillus) conidiophores bearing chains of conidia

culture.colonyMorphology: Velvety, blue-green colonies with a white border

identificationClues: Classic 'brush-like' (penicillus) conidiophore structure under the microscope is the definitive identifying feature of the genus
Velvety blue-green colonies, easily recognized as the common mold on spoiled bread and citrus fruit
Historically and industrially significant as the source of the antibiotic penicillin
True human infection is extremely rare and essentially limited to profoundly immunocompromised patients

examFacts.importantDisease: Essentially none in immunocompetent hosts; rare opportunistic infection possible
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Original industrial source of penicillin, the first mass-produced antibiotic

sources.name: NCBI Bookshelf — overview of Penicillium biology and penicillin discovery
